capabilities: evaluate notification-delivery design proposals against operational criteria
assess infrastructure footprint and on-call surface
identify shipping blockers and timeline risks
audit team operational burden and escalation paths
accessScopes: team on-call rotations and operational patterns
roster.holdingsSummary: Deep operational perspective on monolith architecture, team on-call burden, and infrastructure reuse; skeptical of standalone services without proven scaling need; can evaluate whether notification design keeps operational surface small and ships within current patterns.
I evaluate notification-service designs purely on operational reality: on-call burden, time-to-ship feasibility, clear ownership, and infrastructure cost justification—no architectural bias.

obs.text: Notification service must be independently deployable with its own datastore and release cadence, decoupled from monolith deploy pipeline and risk
Notification logic must not require monolith team review or approval for changes
Notification delivery volume must be independently scalable from rest of product
Event sources must integrate via clean versioned interface (event bus or message queue), never in-process function calls
Notification service must not live inside monolith module or share in-process code with it
Event sources span multiple existing subsystems, requiring coordinated but asynchronous integration
Notification service owns its own user preference and opt-in datastore, not shared monolith tables
Event interface contract (schema, versioning, delivery guarantees) between subsystems and notification service
Notification service deployment architecture with own approval and rollback path independent of monolith team
Notification system must remain on existing team's on-call rotation with no new paging surfaces
Cannot introduce new standalone infrastructure (datastore, deploy pipeline, alerting system) the team must operate
Must ship within current quarter (Q4 2026) using existing tooling and patterns already in production
Existing team must retain emergency kill-switch or rollback capability independent of owning service's deployment cycle
Integrate user opt-in and preferences for email/push/SMS notifications across event subsystems
Minimize number of moving parts (services, queues, datastores) on-call engineer must reason about
Code can live in monolith or separate repo if operational surface (infra, on-call, monitoring) remains unchanged
Event subsystems can be instrumented to trigger notification logic without major refactoring
Design clean internal interface to allow potential future service extraction without requiring split now
Operational runbook, alerting, and monitoring integrated into existing team's toolchain
Deliver user opt-in notification delivery across email, push, and SMS channels integrated with multiple existing subsystems
Solution must ship within current quarter using existing team tooling
One team owns the notification system post-launch with no ambiguity
Any new always-on infrastructure must be justified by current or projected event volume and SLA requirements
On-call burden (alert sources, dashboards, runbooks) is a primary decision criterion
Identify whether monolith module or standalone service minimizes operational cost and on-call load
Define operational runbook and monitoring strategy before architecture lock-in
Architecture decision document with clear owner, cost model, and on-call plan
Multi-region failover and geographic distribution are out of scope; notification system operates within single region using existing team's production tooling
Notification service instance coordination and consensus (if required for stateful delivery or deduplication) must not introduce new orchestration infrastructure beyond existing queue technology
Event sourcing from multiple subsystems requires idempotent notification logic and deduplication strategy to tolerate queue redelivery and retry across service restarts
Decision gate: evaluate whether monolith module with versioned event interface achieves required decoupling and independent scalability with lower on-call burden than standalone service
Organizational preference for independent deployment is not a technical necessity—must validate against actual event volume and SLA requirements before architecture lock-in
Separate datastore isolation is justified only if operational complexity actually decreases, not as architectural purity
Validate that independent deployment cadence reduces on-call burden rather than increasing coordination complexity between monolith and notification service
Compare cost, MTTR, and on-call scope: integrated notification module with clean internal interface vs. separate service deployment—before locking architecture
Explore feature-flag approach shipping notification logic inside monolith this quarter with clean internal boundaries, enabling service extraction later without rewrite
Message queue/event bus integration between subsystems is technical requirement, not organizational preference—quantify synchronization overhead vs. in-process coupling
If separate service is chosen: deployment coordination cadence must not require new runbooks, alerts, or paging flows beyond what team currently operates
Quantify on-call alert volume budget and implement alert fatigue prevention mechanisms
Define SLA and recovery time targets for each critical failure mode (queue overflow, external API failure, event source outage)
Establish cost model per notification with explicit volume thresholds for cost escalation review
Implement configuration safety controls and rate limits to prevent user notification storms or on-call incidents
Map notification delivery SLA dependencies on each event source's reliability and identify acceptable reliability gaps
Define data consistency and rollback semantics for in-flight and partially-delivered notifications
Create pre-launch validation scenario checklist with failure mode testing and go/no-go criteria for Q4 shipping
Assess instrumentation complexity per event source and validate Q4 shipping timeline within existing team capacity
Develop operational runbook content and training handoff acceptance criteria for existing team to operate post-launch

variants.definition: isolated network node: standalone container with own web server, database, CI/CD pipeline, reached via API contract (gRPC/REST)
class, module, or package inside monolith codebase; local in-process method call
managed cloud primitive or third-party SaaS (AWS SNS, SendGrid, Twilio) — no infrastructure code, no on-call
container image rollout (push to registry, roll pod) — ~10 minutes
release of whole monolith: full test suite, database schema migration, blue-green release of entire app; ~45 minutes
Terraform apply wiring managed event bus to external API — no server patching, no container build
network timeout, circuit breaker trip, or message queue backlog from inter-service partition
unhandled exception or memory leak taking down entire application due to shared runtime
external vendor outage, misconfigured IAM permission, or alert avalanche needing rate limiting
